doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Lean playing style and leaving space
summary: He prefers few, meaningful notes and learned from Detroit elders to play the trumpet part and leave room in ensembles.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well I like the fact that on your little breaks that you had in there, you didn’t choose to just fill them with a million notes, like sometimes younger players do. That’s what Cal Collins told me this morning, he said it.

Well it’s true. Yeah, I like to play a more, kind of a lean style, and just try and make the notes count a little bit more, you know, the ones that I play. I’ve never been much of the player who tries to play a zillion notes. And I think especially in the older styles or whatever you want to call it — swing or traditional jazz — it’s less appropriate anyway. It just doesn’t sound right when the trumpet player is playing a zillion notes, especially when you’re playing in the ensembles and playing the lead melody. I learned early on from some of the older guys beating it into me, saying, you know, if you’re going to be playing during ensembles, if you play the trumpet, you play the trumpet part and don’t play all the fills, you know there’s two or three other horn players around who have their roles to do, and so if you can just play a nice, simple, tasteful melody that leaves holes, leaves space, that’s one of the best early lessons I learned from the guys around Detroit and I try to remember that. That’s what makes it work. Everybody has to do their part and leave room for the other guys to do their part. So it’s something I try to think about.
